messages.body_plain:
What do you mean by 'determine the degrees'? The degrees vector is just a vector of normal degrees between 0 and 90, where each value essentially applies a weight argument to collapse the multidimensional information into a scalar value (0 would include the full contribution of a latent trait, while 90 would include no contribution). I think work by Mark Reckase is a good place to look for extra information on this topic. Cheers.

Phil

Hi, Phil:

I'm trying to replicate the rasch analysis of some data (20 items and 500 observations) that was computed with Bilog MG. My first choice was mirt but I have tried with eRm and ltm too. The better aproximation has been mirt model with all default arguments but QMCEM method. In average, differences in item's difficults are -0.017.

The problem is itemfit, I tried the three different methods for itemfit with X2 and S_X2 but, based on p.value, I can´t obtain a fitting that match with that of Bilog.

I know the X2 of Bilog is not the same statistic that mirt's X2 but I considered that there must be some correspondence since both analysis are, in essence, rasch model.

Any idea?

Thanks in advance

Questions about BILOG seem to be coming up more and more now, and the truth is I have no interest in matching results with that program. I'm sure it's good, but to me it seems rather dated compared to more recent software.

In principle the approaches BILOG and mirt use are the same, though of course how the binning occurs is slightly different. However, I don't think using the X2 fit statistics is ever a good idea, primarily because it is extremely conservative and limited only to unidimensional models (unless you have massive sample sizes, in which case multidimensional binning may be possible). See the attached simulation study for an example emulating the data you are currently exploring. You notice that the X2 never comes close to the nominal alpha rate of .05 for Type I errors (while the S-X2 does), and in the case where the item does have some misfit it's power to detect this is extremely low, especially when compared to S-X2 which is more powerful by orders of magnitude. I have no doubt that you'll come to the same conclusion when running this simulation with BILOG as well.

Phil

Hi Steven,

Sometimes lattice plots can be quite annoying. Worst case you can always extract elements for the object directly and build a custom plot (there some examples of this in the forum, in case you're interested).

trellis.par.set(list(plot.line = list(col = "black")))

I see. This is a different kind of error that's slightly harder to solve. Currently the parameter vector is actually smaller than you think because linear constraints are being tracked internally for the grsm types (hence the error). So, considerably fewer unique parameters are being tracked, all redundant intercepts in this case.

The easiest solution would be to remove all constraints when these special optimizers are used, however that means that users would have to supply the rating scale model constraints as well, which tend to be cumbersome and are largely automatic (and could cause optimizers like this to choke due to the higher dimensional search....though don't quote me on that).

Perhaps I'll add a technical argument to disable all internal constraints so that it's more clear what is going on. There's already and option like this for mixedmirt(), so might as well make it available elsewhere. Cheers.

Phil

You'll notice that multipleGroup() has a ... argument, meaning that other arguments not found in this documentation can be passed. help(mirt) contains the other possible arguments that can be passed to this function, one of which is survey.weights. What you need to do is supply a vector of weights for each case, where the sum of this vector is equal to the number of rows in your data. E.g., if you wanted the first half of your responses to be worth three times as much as the second half of the responses then survey.weights <- c(rep(3/2, N/2), rep(1/2, 2/N)). Supplying this to multipleGroup() will weight the likelihood accordingly, and from there you can use Wald or likelihood-ratio comparisons for DIF. HTH.

Phil

P.S. You definitely don't want configural invariance for DIF testing. Choose a set of anchor items and free the latent variance/mean terms to equate the groups, then continue with DIF. Otherwise your tests will contain population drift effects, and therefore DIF testing will be inappropriate.
